results.title: Burnside's theorem on matrix algebras
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, $n$ a natural number, and $A$ a $k$-subalgebra of the algebra $M_n(k)$ of $n \times n$ matrices over $k$. Suppose that the only subspaces $W$ of $k^n$ with $Mv \in W$ for all $M \in A$ and all $v \in W$ are $0$ and $k^n$. Then $A = M_n(k)$.

results.title: Frobenius theorem on real division algebras
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional associative unital division algebra over $\mathbb{R}$. Then $A$ is isomorphic as an $\mathbb{R}$-algebra to $\mathbb{R}$, to $\mathbb{C}$, or to the algebra $\mathbb{H}$ of real quaternions.

results.title: Skolem–Noether theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be a finite-dimensional central simple algebra over $k$. Then every $k$-algebra automorphism $\sigma$ of $A$ is inner: there is a unit $u \in A^\times$ such that $\sigma(x) = u x u^{-1}$ for all $x \in A$.

results.title: Character values of a finite group lie in a cyclotomic field

results.title: Orbit-normalized weights give equal nonnegative integrals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Nonnegative integrals of an invariant function agree for orbit-normalized weights. Normalization is needed only where the function is nonzero, and the common integral is allowed to be infinite.

results.title: Integrability is independent of the orbit-normalized weight
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Integrability of an invariant complex function times a nonnegative real weight is independent of the weight when both orbit averages are one on the function's support. Neither weighted function is required to be integrable.

results.title: Orbit-normalized cutoffs give equal complex integrals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Weighted integrals of an invariant complex function agree for nonnegative orbit-normalized cutoffs. If one weighted function is not integrable, neither is the other, and both Bochner integrals are zero.

results.title: Subgroup-normalized weights give equal integrals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Subgroup-normalized nonnegative weights give the same integral of an invariant complex function. This measure-theoretic statement requires neither a closed subgroup nor compact supports nor a bounded function.

results.title: Continuous cutoff for a closed-embedding homomorphism
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A continuous nonnegative compactly supported cutoff normalized on every left orbit meeting `K`, for a closed-embedding homomorphism `ι`. The measure may have any scale. No Hausdorff or countability hypotheses are required.

results.title: Continuous Bruhat cutoff for a closed subgroup
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Existence of a Bruhat section for a closed subgroup
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A Bruhat section: given a closed subgroup `T` of a locally compact group and a set `E` contained in `T * C` for compact `C`, there is a compactly supported nonnegative measurable function `w` whose integral over each `T`-translate meeting `E` equals `1`.

results.title: Bounded invariant functions are integrable against normalized cutoffs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A bounded measurable `T`-invariant complex function is integrable against any nonnegative measurable compactly supported weight whose `T`-average is one wherever the function is nonzero. The weight need not be bounded.

results.title: Cutoff independence of integrals of bounded invariant functions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The integral of a bounded measurable `T`-invariant complex function against a nonnegative measurable compactly supported cutoff does not depend on the cutoff, when each cutoff has subgroup integral one on the support of that function. Normalization is not required outside its support.

results.title: Positive common integral of cocompact subgroup cutoffs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A compact cocompactness witness gives a continuous normalized cutoff and a positive common integral for all nonnegative measurable compactly supported normalized cutoffs. Every such cutoff is genuinely integrable, even when it is not bounded. Neither the ambient group nor the subgroup must be Hausdorff.

results.title: Existence of a locally constant normalized subgroup cutoff
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A compact set in a topological group with a compact open subgroup has a nonnegative locally constant cutoff whose integral over every left `T`-orbit meeting that set is one, for a closed commutative subgroup `T`. The same compactly supported function works simultaneously on all of `T * Ω`. The Haar measure need not have any prescribed normalization.

results.title: Factor of an infinite word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A right-infinite word over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a sequence $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ of letters $u_n \in \alpha$. For natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $i$ is the word $u_i u_{i+1} \cdots u_{i+k-1}$, given as the map $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_{i+s}$.

results.title: Set of factors of a given length
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and a natural number $k$, the set of length-$k$ factors of $u$ is the set of the maps $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_{i+s}$, for $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: Initial segment of an infinite word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and a natural number $k$, the length-$k$ initial segment of $u$ is the word $u_0 u_1 \cdots u_{k-1}$, given as the map $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, $s \mapsto u_s$; it is the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $0$.

results.title: Finitely many factors of each length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the alphabet $\alpha$ is finite, then for every right-infinite word $u$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $k$, the set of length-$k$ factors of $u$ is finite.

results.title: Factor as a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the length-$k$ factor of $u$ at position $i$, as a list, is $[u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+k-1}]$ (the empty list when $k = 0$).

results.title: Lists occurring in an infinite word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite list $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a factor of a right-infinite word $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ over $\alpha$ when, writing $\ell$ for the length of $w$, there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ with $w = [u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+\ell-1}]$. In particular, the empty list is a factor of every right-infinite word over $\alpha$.

results.title: Nonempty factors of an infinite word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ be a right-infinite word over an alphabet $\alpha$, viewed as a map $\mathbb{N} \to \alpha$. A finite word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ over $\alpha$ is a nonempty factor of $u$ when $n \ge 1$ and there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $w_j = u_{i+j}$ for every $j < n$.

results.title: Occurrence via list-valued factors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be a finite list of length $\ell$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and $u$ a right-infinite word over $\alpha$. Then $w$ is a factor of $u$ if and only if there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the length-$\ell$ factor of $u$ at position $i$, as a list, equals $w$.

results.title: Nonempty factors via list-valued factors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be a finite list of length $\ell$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ a right-infinite word over $\alpha$. Then $w$ is a nonempty factor of $u$ if and only if $w$ is nonempty and there is a position $i \in \mathbb{N}$ with $[u_i, u_{i+1}, \ldots, u_{i+\ell-1}] = w$.

results.title: Nonempty factors are the factors that are nonempty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a finite list $w$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ and a right-infinite word $u$ over $\alpha$, $w$ is a nonempty factor of $u$ if and only if $w$ is nonempty and $w$ is a factor of $u$.

results.title: Factors as lists and as tuples agree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number, $v$ a map $\{0, \ldots, k-1\} \to \alpha$, written $j \mapsto v_j$, and $u$ a right-infinite word over $\alpha$. Then the list $[v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_{k-1}]$ is a factor of $u$ if and only if $v$ belongs to the set of length-$k$ factors of $u$. This holds also for $k = 0$.

results.title: Factor complexity of an infinite word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$. For $n \ge 0$ and a position $i \ge 0$, the factor of $w$ of length $n$ at position $i$ is the word $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_{i+n-1}$. The factor complexity $p_w(n)$ is the number of distinct factors of $w$ of length $n$, each word being counted once however often it occurs in $w$.

results.title: Factor complexity at length zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every infinite word $w$ over a finite alphabet, the factor complexity of $w$ at length $0$ equals $1$, that is, $p_w(0) = 1$: the empty word is the only factor of $w$ of length $0$.

results.title: Rook graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the rook graph on the $n \times m$ board is the simple graph whose vertices are the cells $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which two cells are adjacent if and only if they are distinct and lie in the same row (same $i$) or the same column (same $j$).

results.title: Dominating sets of the rook graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, a finite set $S$ of cells of the $n \times m$ board dominates the rook graph on that board if and only if for every cell $(i, j)$, some cell of $S$ lies in row $i$ or some cell of $S$ lies in column $j$.

results.title: Rook placements covering all rows and columns
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $m$ and $k$, $E_{n,m}(k)$ is the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that contain a cell in every row and a cell in every column (Mertens' $E_{n,m}(k)$).

results.title: Dominating rook placements
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$, $m$ and $k$, $d_{n,m}(k)$ is the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook graph on that board (Mertens' $d_{R_{n,m}}(k)$).

results.title: Domination polynomial of the rook graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the rook domination polynomial of the $n \times m$ board is the integer polynomial $D_{n,m}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{nm} d_{n,m}(k)\, x^k$, where $d_{n,m}(k)$ is the number of $k$-element sets of cells of the $n \times m$ board that are dominating sets of the rook graph on that board.

results.title: Closed straight-line system
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A closed straight-line system: one defining term per variable, plus a query formula. The definition at position `k` is the definition of variable `k`. There are no free input variables: every variable the system talks about must be defined by the system itself.

results.title: Acyclic closed straight-line system
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A closed straight-line system is acyclic when every defining term mentions only earlier variables, and the query mentions only defined variables. Hence every variable occurring anywhere in the system is defined, and unfolding the definitions terminates at ground terms: there is no free input variable.

results.title: Satisfaction of a closed straight-line system
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Satisfaction of a closed straight-line system: the assignment obeys every definition and satisfies the query.

results.title: One fold step of straight-line evaluation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: One fold step: evaluate the next defining term under the values computed so far and append the result.

results.title: Folded assignment values of a straight-line system
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The folded assignment values, in variable order.

results.title: Candidate assignment of a straight-line system
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The candidate assignment of a straight-line system.

results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Orthogonal projection
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A continuous linear operator $P$ on a complex Hilbert space $H$ is an orthogonal projection if it is idempotent, $P^2 = P$, and self-adjoint, $P^* = P$.

results.title: Frame function on projections
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. A frame function on the projection lattice of $H$ is a function $\mu$ from the continuous linear operators on $H$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that $\mu(P) \ge 0$ for every orthogonal projection $P$ on $H$, $\mu(P + Q) = \mu(P) + \mu(Q)$ for all orthogonal projections $P$ and $Q$ on $H$ with $PQ = 0$, and $\mu(I) = 1$ for the identity operator $I$ on $H$.

results.title: Real part of the trace
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a continuous linear operator $A$ on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $H$, let $\operatorname{tr}(A) \in \mathbb{C}$ be the trace of $A$ as a $\mathbb{C}$-linear map on $H$. The real part of the trace of $A$ is the real number $\operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr}(A)$.

results.title: Gleason's theorem in finite dimensions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension at least $3$, write $\operatorname{tr}$ for the trace of a $\mathbb{C}$-linear map on $H$, and let $\mu$ be a frame function on the projection lattice of $H$. Then there is a unique continuous linear operator $\rho$ on $H$ such that $\rho$ is positive, $\operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr}(\rho) = 1$, and…

results.title: Frame function on the unit sphere
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. A frame function on the unit sphere of $H$ is a function $f$ from the unit vectors of $H$ to $\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x) \ge 0$ for every unit vector $x$ in $H$ and, for every Hilbert basis $(b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of $H$, the family $(f(b_i))_{i \in \iota}$ is unconditionally summable with sum $1$.

results.title: Gleason's theorem for separable Hilbert spaces
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a separable complex Hilbert space whose dimension over $\mathbb{C}$ is at least $3$, and let $f$ be a frame function on the unit sphere of $H$. Then there is a positive continuous linear operator $\rho$ on $H$ such that $f(x) = \operatorname{Re} \langle x, \rho x \rangle$ for every unit vector $x$ in $H$.

results.title: Explicit solution of the logistic equation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Explicit solution of the logistic equation `x' = r x (1 - x / K)` with `x 0 = x₀`: `K x₀ e^{r t} / (K + x₀ (e^{r t} - 1))`.

results.title: Initial value of the logistic solution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The logistic solution starts at `x₀` (for `K ≠ 0`).

results.title: Positivity of the logistic solution's denominator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In the biological domain (`K > 0`, `x₀ > 0`, `r t ≥ 0`, or `x₀ ≤ K`) the denominator of the logistic solution is positive.

results.title: The explicit solution solves the logistic equation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Wherever the denominator `K + x₀ (e^{r t} - 1)` is nonzero, `x' = r x (1 - x / K)` (all real parameters, `K ≠ 0`).

results.title: Uniqueness of the logistic solution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Uniqueness of the logistic solution on `[0, T]`: in the biological domain (`K > 0`, `x₀ > 0`, `r ≥ 0`), any function continuous on `[0, T]`, with right derivative `r x (1 - x / K)` on `[0, T)` and `x 0 = x₀`, equals the explicit solution on `[0, T]`.

results.title: Convergence to the carrying capacity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `r > 0` and `x₀ > 0`, `x(t) → K` as `t → ∞` (the identity needs no sign condition on `K`; biologically `K > 0`).

results.title: Exponential limit
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For fixed `r`, `x₀`, `t`, the logistic solution tends to the exponential-growth solution `x₀ e^{r t}` as the carrying capacity `K → ∞`.

results.title: Log-odds grow linearly
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Log-odds grow linearly for a frequency (`K = 1`): for `0 < x₀ < 1` and all `r`, `t`, `log (x(t) / (1 - x(t))) = log (x₀ / (1 - x₀)) + r t`.

results.title: Exact deterministic transit time
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Starting from frequency `a ∈ (0, 1)` with `r ≠ 0`, the logistic frequency reaches `1 - a` at time `(2 / r) log ((1 - a) / a)`.

results.title: Logistic transit time from $1/(2N)$ to $1 - 1/(2N)$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The transit time from `1 / (2N)` to `1 - 1 / (2N)` is `(2 / r) log (2N - 1)`, for `N ≥ 1` and `r ≠ 0`.

results.title: Logistic solution is strictly increasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `r > 0` and `0 < x₀ < K` the logistic solution is strictly increasing, so the transit time of `logistic_transitTime` is the unique time at which `1 - a` is reached.
